A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FAST research despite the changed title and extensive reorganization. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices support reliable matching and comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original SAE reconstruction experiments, automated feature-interpretability evaluations, steering outputs and training trajectories across Llama and Qwen models.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds GSNR measurements, behavioral-fidelity evaluations, controlled ablations, training-time measurements and activation-distribution analyses.

M1.justification: FAST retains independent chat-templated sequence processing, Standard and JumpReLU SAE objectives, and the shuffled half-buffer training cycle. Expanded initialization and steering descriptions do not establish procedural changes. Appendix B explicitly introduces its smoothed objective only for theoretical analysis.

E1.justification: The instruction-data mixture, Pile baseline data and steering tasks are retained. Section 5.5 adds an input scenario with an unrelated 512-token prefix. Qwen2.5-Math-7B is an additional evaluated model, but no separate mathematics dataset or task is specified.

E2.justification: BT(P) and BT(F) remain the principal comparators. v2 adds RandomConcat as an evaluated comparison variant against clean FAST in the controlled-prefix experiment, Table 17. Newly discussed RouteSAE, SAIF and low-rank approaches are not experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds early-training GSNR evaluation, Delta Loss and KL metrics, a matched 2048-token context control, and a controlled 512-token-prefix protocol. It also evaluates Qwen2.5-Math-7B at four layers. These substantially extend the evaluation design while retaining the original 40.96-million-token training budget and principal reconstruction settings.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether context length or unrelated predecessor text explains FAST's advantage, examine activation-strength distributions, and compare training efficiency. Conversely, v1 Appendix G's loss, sparsity, dead-feature, explained-variance and CE-score trajectories are removed. The existing steering case studies are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions disclose seed 42 without repeated-run counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The added GSNR values diagnose training-gradient signal and noise; they do not introduce uncertainty estimates for comparative performance results.

E6.justification: v1's reconstruction Tables 3–9 are numerically retained as v2 Tables 6–12, and the original interpretability and steering results remain. New results cover GSNR, context/prefix controls, Qwen2.5-Math, Delta Loss, KL, timing and activation distributions. FAST has the lowest KL in 11 of 12 configurations, with Qwen2.5-7B layer 20 an exception. Earlier training-trajectory results are removed.

T1.justification: v2 adds a formal attention-contamination definition, a zero-mean/uncorrelated-noise assumption, a variance-decomposition lemma and a GSNR-degradation theorem with proofs. Appendix B adds surrogate-objective assumptions, a nonconvex SGD convergence derivation and an efficiency-ratio corollary, explicitly distinguishing these bounds from guarantees for the implemented Adam training.

C1.justification: The reconstruction, interpretability and special-token steering contributions remain. v2 elevates attention contamination and destructive gradient noise into a central theoretical contribution in the abstract and introduction, and adds headline claims about higher GSNR and near-zero Delta Loss. The paper's claimed contribution therefore extends beyond the original empirical training proposal.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations based on attention leakage, contrasting base/instruct data regimes, activation stability and padding-related efficiency. It qualifies the theoretical analysis as conditional and partly an SGD proxy, but removes v1's explicit empirical limitations concerning model scale, strongly activated feature selection and preliminary steering evidence. Its universal performance language also exceeds the KL results, which contain a Qwen2.5-7B exception.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies the 262,144-activation buffer, reports training times and clarifies deterministic steering-feature selection. It omits v1's exact GPT-4o snapshot, 128-feature sampling and 4,608-score counts, greedy-decoding disclosure, and data/240-checkpoint availability statements. Most training hyperparameters and the code link remain unchanged; these documentation changes do not establish altered underlying experiments or resource availability.

R1.justification: v2 adds RouteSAE, SAIF and low-rank adaptation discussion, positioning FAST as complementary to architectural approaches. GSNR and stochastic-optimization references newly ground its central argument, while the earlier Kissane dataset-dependence/refusal discussion and citations disappear. This substantively changes the research positioning beyond bibliographic updates to retained works.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, related work, interpretability discussion, steering section and conclusion undergo extensive rewriting. Theory and motivation become separate sections, while background and substantial steering explanations move into reorganized appendices. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, adds an attention-contamination diagram and numerous comparison tables, relocates existing material, and removes the training-log panels. v2 Figure 5 incorrectly displays Standard-SAE reconstruction curves under a JumpReLU caption, replacing v1's appropriate JumpReLU plot; the architecture-specific appendix tables remain intact.

improvement.justification: The matched-context ablation addresses an important confound in v1, the controlled-prefix experiment tests the proposed mechanism, and Delta Loss/KL add direct behavioral-fidelity evidence. These strengthen the scientific support. However, the gains are tempered by removed limitations and reproducibility details, lost training trajectories, the incorrect Figure 5, and universal performance claims contradicted by the Qwen2.5-7B KL results. The net quality improvement is therefore limited despite the substantial revision.
